extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, and in-house counsel (particularly biotech/pharma practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the Section 112 enablement requirement, especially for genus (class-wide) claims such as broadly claimed antibodies. Focuses on how much disclosure and guidance a specification must provide to make and use the claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable the full scope of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: “The specification must enable the full scope of the invention as defined by its claims.” (Slip op. at 13.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class. The Court emphasized: “the more a party claims, the broader the monopoly it demands, the more it must enable.” This principle applies across technology areas (telegraphs, glues, antibodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory enablement standard (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must describe the invention “in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art . . . to make and use the [invention].”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is judged against this statutory language. The requirement is to enable 'make and use' of the invention to a person of ordinary skill in the art; courts will interpret whether the disclosure meets this statutory floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims require more than a few narrow working examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to a broad genus cannot be supported solely by a small number of working examples purporting to fall within that genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Amgen, claiming millions of antibodies while disclosing only 26 sequences was held insufficient. A specification must provide adequate guidance beyond narrow examples to enable the full claimed class; reliance solely on a small representative set is an inadequate basis for a broad monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: A few examples may suffice only if a general quality running through the class is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: “It may suffice to give an example (or a few examples) if the specification also discloses ‘some general quality . . . running through’ the class that gives it ‘a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose.’” (Slip op. at 13.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will accept limited examples when the specification identifies a unifying property or 'general quality' across the claimed class that enables practitioners to recognize or make other members of the class without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable experimentation is permitted but has limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use a patented invention, but what is reasonable depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art. (Slip op. at 15.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement tolerates some experimentation, but courts distinguish reasonable follow-up work from undue or 'painstaking' experimentation. Analysis is context-specific: in some arts, modest experimentation is normal; in others, extensive trial-and-error indicates a lack of enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial-and-error research assignments are not enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that amount to advice to generate and test many candidates (i.e., 'research assignments' or instruction to engage in trial-and-error) do not satisfy enablement. The Court described Amgen’s roadmap and conservative substitution approaches as “little more than two research assignments” and “little more than advice to engage in ‘trial and error.’” (Slip op. at 16–18.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roadmaps that tell practitioners to create a wide range of molecules and test them, or to make systematic substitutions followed by empirical testing, are problematic if success is uncertain given the state of the art. Such guidance is an anti-pattern for enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot force 'painstaking experimentation' to make the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcing a scientist to engage in 'painstaking experimentation' to see what works is not enablement; it is more like providing 'a hunting license.' (Slip op. at 18.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the path from disclosure to practicing the full claimed scope requires extensive, unpredictable trial-and-error, courts are likely to find lack of enablement. The boundary between reasonable and 'painstaking' experimentation is evaluated case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement depends on the state of the art and the nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as adequate disclosure and a reasonable degree of experimentation 'will depend on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment requires technical judgment about whether, given the contemporaneous state of knowledge, the specification provides sufficient guidance to make and use the claimed scope without undue effort. If success is an 'uncertain prospect given the state of the art,' enablement is less likely to be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may decide enablement as a matter of law where no reasonable factfinder could find adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit held that 'no reasonable factfinder could conclude' Amgen provided adequate guidance beyond the 26 working examples, leading to a decision as a matter of law that the claims are not enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement can be resolved at summary judgment or on the pleadings if the record shows that even taking evidence in the light most favorable, the specification cannot support the claimed scope. Practitioners should be aware of the risk of early termination of claims on enablement grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not disclose every embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 does not require that the specification describe how to make and use every single embodiment within a claimed class; examples can be sufficient in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limiting principle to balance the 'full scope' rule: courts will consider whether the examples plus disclosed general principles are enough to enable the rest without undue experimentation.
